name: Domaine de la Janasse Châteauneuf-du-Pape Vieilles Vignes 2012
text:
## Domaine de la Janasse Châteauneuf-du-Pape Vieilles Vignes 2012

**The story.** Domaine de la Janasse is a family estate based in [Courthézon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Domaine+de+la+Janasse,+Courth%C3%A9zon,+France&t=k), one of the five communes of the [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC) appellation. It is young by the village's standards: from 1967 the family's grapes were sold in bulk to merchants, and only in 1973 did Aimé Sabon found the domaine and start making the wine himself. The name comes from a small parcel of vines called La Janasse. In 2001 Aimé's children, Christophe and Isabelle, joined him to run the estate ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

Aimé gradually built up 15 hectares in Châteauneuf, spread over 15 parcels on different soils, plus about 40 hectares in the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC). The year 1990 was a milestone: the first time Janasse made all three of its red Châteauneufs. Janasse is known for a modern, polished style. Since 1993 it has destemmed most of its grapes; [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) ferments in concrete and ages in large old casks (foudres), while [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) and [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah) ferment in conical oak vats and age partly in new French [oak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oak_%28wine%29) barrels ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**The wine: Vieilles Vignes.** "Vieilles vignes" means old vines, and this is Janasse's top red, from vines 60 to over 100 years old, mostly on the big rounded stones, the [galets roulés](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galets_roul%C3%A9s), with some sand and clay. The oldest vines are in [La Crau](https://www.google.com/maps?q=La+Crau,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k). Wine Enthusiast describes it as a blend from four distinct vineyard sites, with vines dating as far back as 1920 ([JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2019-domaine-de-la-janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-vieilles-vignes/2019-3868-750/)). The usual blend is about 85% Grenache, 10% Syrah and a little Mourvèdre and [Cinsault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cinsaut). About two-thirds of the grapes are destemmed and the rest fermented as whole bunches. The wine then ages three-quarters in foudres and a quarter in demi-muids (large barrels), 40% of them new. About 850 cases are made ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

Jeff Leve's honest caution: some tasters love this cuvée young, but he finds the oak can overwhelm the Grenache in some vintages when the wine is young. "Patience is virtue here", he writes, because it is truly worth the wait.

For 2012, Jeb Dunnuck gives the blend as 85% Grenache, 10% Mourvèdre and the rest Syrah, aged in a mix of foudre and barrels; Jeff Leve reports 80/10/10 and 15.5% alcohol. Decanter adds that part of the wine is aged in 600-litre barrels ([JJ Buckley, critics' notes](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2012-domaine-de-la-janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-vieilles-vignes/2012-3868-750/)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/southern-rhone) calls 2012 in the southern Rhône "much more successful than 2011". It was a low-acid year with roughly average alcohol, volumes down by up to 15%, and kind weather late in the season let growers pick without hurry; the wines combine ripeness with some freshness and were expected to peak in their teens. For Janasse it was a banner year: the Wine Advocate put this wine "up in the top handful of wines in the vintage".

**What the critics say for 2012.** As listed by [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/wine/2012-domaine-de-la-janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-vieilles-vignes/2012-3868-750/):
- **[Jeb Dunnuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeb_Dunnuck): 96** (February 2018). One of his favourite wines "in just about every vintage": black fruits, crushed rocks, [garrigue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Garrigue) and violets; full-bodied, concentrated and beautifully balanced, with ripe tannin. "A joy to drink", with another 10 to 15-plus years ahead.
- **Jeff Leve, [The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/): 96** (September 2014). Rich, long and deep, with layers of ripe, peppery sweet black raspberries. "A very good wine in any vintage, but it's a real superstar in 2012!"
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 96** (Jeb Dunnuck, October 2014). A rich, layered Châteauneuf "that doesn't put a foot wrong": blackberry, liquid violets, spice and serious minerality, with awesome mid-palate depth and sweet tannin. It would "thrill through 2027".
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 96** (James Molesworth, October 2014). Tightly coiled then: anise, blackberry coulis, plum paste and macerated fig, with black tea, smouldering tobacco and warm ganache; long, dense but very silky, with violet and [pastis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastis) in the background. Best 2017 to 2035.
- **[Decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decanter_%28magazine%29): 94** (September 2019). From vines over 100 years old: remarkably perfumed and lifted, with spicy red fruit and light toastiness; powerful yet tight and elegant, with fine-grained tannins and "no burn on the finish" despite the high alcohol.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 92.9** (from your CellarTracker list).

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is fourteen years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2020 to 2027, and the Wine Advocate's ran to 2027, though Wine Spectator's runs to 2035 and Dunnuck (in 2018) saw 10 to 15-plus more years. So it is fully mature: drink it over the next year or two rather than holding it. Expect the oak Leve warned about to have melted into kirsch, pepper, leather and garrigue. Decant gently, mainly to leave the sediment behind.

**Serving.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests about 15.5°C, almost cellar temperature, and 1 to 2 hours in a [decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) to soften the wine and open its perfume; older bottles need only enough to leave the sediment behind. It says Janasse is usually best with 4 to 6 years in bottle, and the best vintages drink well from 4 to 18 years after the harvest ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).

**Food.** The Wine Cellar Insider suggests classic meat dishes (veal, pork, beef, lamb, duck, game, roast chicken, braises, sausages, barbecue and [cassoulet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassoulet)), plus mushrooms, eggplant, cheese and tomatoes. My picks: a slow-cooked lamb [tagine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tagine) with dried fruit, a beef [daube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daube), [venison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venison) with a juniper or pepper sauce, or a mushroom dish with black olive [tapenade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapenade). I'd avoid delicate fish and very spicy food.

**Value and where to buy.** None of the three stores on this site lists Janasse Vieilles Vignes at the moment. It turns up with merchants such as [JJ Buckley](https://www.jjbuckley.com/), often on pre-arrival, and at auction. For a wine regularly scored 97 to 99, it is good value among top Châteauneufs.

**From the history books**
- **The popes and their castle.** In 1309 [Pope Clement V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_Clement_V) moved the papacy to [Avignon](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Palais+des+Papes,+Avignon,+France&t=k), beginning the [Avignon Papacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avignon_Papacy). His successor [John XXII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_XXII) improved the vineyards to the north and built the summer [castle](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+des+Papes,+Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+France&t=k) that gave the village its name ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **France's first appellation.** Fraud was so common in the early 20th century that local growers, led by Baron [Pierre Le Roy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Le_Roy_de_Boiseaumari%C3%A9) of [Château Fortia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Fortia), drew up France's first [appellation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appellation_d'origine_contr%C3%B4l%C3%A9e) rules in 1923, made law in 1936 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **From bulk to bottle.** Before World War I, much Châteauneuf was sold in bulk to [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) to beef up thinner wines ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)). At Janasse, bulk sales lasted much longer: the family sold its grapes to merchants until 1973, when Aimé Sabon began bottling under his own name ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **Courthézon.** The estate sits in [Courthézon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courth%C3%A9zon), one of the five communes of the appellation, alongside Châteauneuf-du-Pape, [Bédarrides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9darrides), [Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orange,_Vaucluse) and [Sorgues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sorgues) ([Châteauneuf-du-Pape appellation](https://en.chateauneuf.com/appellation-chateauneuf-du-pape/vintages/chateauneuf-du-pape-2016/)).

**Curious details**
- **Vines from 1912.** Janasse's all-Grenache cuvée, Chaupin, comes from vines planted in 1912 on pure sand ([The Wine Cellar Insider](https://www.thewinecellarinsider.com/rhone-wines-cote-rotie-hermitage-chateauneuf-du-pape/chateauneuf-du-pape-wine-producer-profiles/janasse-chateauneuf-du-pape-rhone-wine/)).
- **XXL.** In 2007 and again in 2016, Janasse made a monster called XXL: old-vine Grenache with a little Mourvèdre from La Crau and Saumade, three years in barrel, 16.5% alcohol, and only about 115 cases.
- **A secret dessert wine.** Janasse makes a tiny amount of [vin de paille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Straw_wine), a sweet wine from grapes dried on straw, sold only at the estate. Jeff Leve wishes he had bought more.
- **The flying-cigar law.** In 1954, after local reports of [UFOs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flying_saucer), the Châteauneuf council banned "flying cigars" from flying over or landing in the commune. The decree is still in force ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Why the blend matters.** In Châteauneuf, [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache) gives sweet, ripe, almost jam-like juice when very ripe; [Syrah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syrah) adds colour and spice; and [Mourvèdre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mourv%C3%A8dre) brings elegance and structure. Grenache covered about 72% of the appellation's vineyards in 2004, Syrah about 10.5% and Mourvèdre only about 7% ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC)).
- **Strong by law.** Châteauneuf must reach at least 12.5% alcohol with no added sugar, and most wines come in at 14 to 15.5%. Yields are limited to 35 hectolitres per hectare, nearly half what Bordeaux allows ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape_AOC); [Bordeaux wine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bordeaux_wine)).
